name: JACKPOT PANDA
iocPatterns: Exploitation of React Server Components via CVE‑2025‑55182 (React2Shell)

Delivery of ransomware payloads (LockBit, Medusa, PlayCrypt)
Compromised IoT devices acting as proxy C2 relays
Obfuscated traffic via fast‑flux domain infrastructure
keyCapabilities: Exploits public–facing application vulnerabilities (e.g., CVE‑2025‑55182), rapid zero‑day deployment
Supply chain compromises via malicious VSCode extensions Custom webshell delivery and maintenance
Advanced RAT deployment (Cobalt Strike, Sliver, Vshell) for C2 and lateral movement
Credential harvesting and legitimate administrative utility exploitation
Double‑extortion ransomware tactics employing LockBit, Medusa, PlayCrypt
Use of compromised IoT devices as Operational Relay Boxes to obfuscate C2 traffic
recommendedActions: Purge or patch all deployments of vulnerable React Server Components (≥ React 19 and Next.js ≥ 16.0.6); monitor for CVE‑2025‑55182 activity; keep frameworks at the latest security patch level.
Implement comprehensive application whitelist and runtime protection that detects unexpected code execution within serverless environments.

Enforce strict zero‑trust network segmentation to limit lateral movement after web‑app compromise. Deploy endpoint detection and response (EDR) solutions capable of identifying RAT families (Cobalt Strike, Sliver), and monitor for unusual PowerShell execution or WMI calls indicative of credential dumping.

campaignsText: Jackpot Panda is highly operationally agile: the group was documented deploying active exploitation of React2Shell within hours of its public disclosure in December 2025, evidencing a rapid threat intelligence‑driven approach. Campaigns are typically short‑circuited—initial intrusion via web‑application exploit, followed by swift lateral movement and deployment of backdoors or ransomware before the target can fully respond. Their victim profiles are wide but skew towards entities with high-value data and operational importance in China’s national interests. Past operations highlighted include a 2020 focus on gambling platforms across South Korea and Vietnam, along with targeted supply‑chain compromises affecting fintech firms in the United States and European markets. Notable adversary families like APT36 and Chaos have been linked through shared toolsets and tactics, indicating possible collaboration or overlapping objectives. The adversary’s preferred infrastructure comprises cloud‑based staging servers, bullet‑proof hosting domains for C2, and fast‑flux DNS to hide command channels, frequently leveraging third‑party content delivery networks (CDNs) such as Amazon Web Services fo
description: Jackpot Panda is a China‑aligned APT that has been active since May 2020, primarily targeting online gambling, financial services and government entities across East and Southeast Asia. The group exploits zero‑day web‑application vulnerabilities such as CVE‑2025‑55182 (React2Shell) to gain initial footholds, then deploys a mix of commercial RATs, custom rootkits and ransomware families for persistence, lateral movement and double‑extortion tactics.
goals: The actor’s strategic objectives appear dual‑pronged: first, to conduct covert intelligence gathering on political, financial, and technical aspects of target organizations that may influence Chinese domestic security or corrupt officials; second, to monetize operations through ransomware payouts. The primary focus on the online gambling ecosystem reflects the Chinese government’s interest in monitoring illicit funds and potential political leverage points. By targeting a wide spectrum of sectors—including finance, defense, healthcare, telecommunications, critical infrastructure, education, media, manufacturing, energy, aerospace, hospitality, retail, non‑profit, maritime, gaming, aviation, transportation, think‑tanks, legal services, utilities, IT, nuclear, entertainment, food‑agriculture, construction and mining—the adversary maximizes the probability of uncovering valuable hard‑copy or digital intelligence while maintaining a broad attack surface for opportunistic monetization. Specific countries—China (CN), Russia (RU), Iran (IR), India (IN), North Korea (KP), Ukraine (UA), United States (US), Brazil (BR), United Kingdom (GB), South Korea (KR), Pakistan (PK), Germany (DE), Turkey (TR), Vietnam (VN), Belarus (BY), Poland (PL), Taiwan (TW), Canada (CA) and Australia (AU)—are targeted in line with China’s geopolitical interests, ensuring a mix of critical national infrastructures and politically sensitive organizations across both domestic and foreign markets. Typical victims are mid‑ to large‑sized enterprises that host web applications exposing React Server Components or other easily exploitable surfaces, and which have valuable data assets such as customer, financial or governmental records.
